text.p: Industrial production in Yugoslavia this year could rise by six percent at the most but four percent is a more realistic figure, the Belgrade-based Institute of Economic Sciences said on Tuesday.
"We forecast industrial output to increase by four percent despite the inflow of unidentified capital from abroad," institute director Tomislav Popovic told a news conference.
The institute's forecast is well below government expectations of a 10.5 percent rise in industrial output.

He said there were certain signs of revival of industrial production in the past months, but added: "This was based on the expansion of loans and money supply M1 as well as on the increasing foreign trade deficit."
Industrial output in July dropped 3.1 percent against the previous month, but cummulative data for the first seven months show an increase of 3.8 percent against the same period 1995.
Stojan Stamenkovic, the leading economist in the institute, said such a trend was just short term.
The expansion of the trade deficit, which in January-August period topped to $1.16 billion, is limited by the available funds held abroad.
Analysts believe Yugoslav authorities have managed to shift large ammounts of hard currency abroad in the early 90's despite a trade and financial noose around the country.
Reliable figures are hard to come by, but the average monthly dificit of about $145 million must be reduced, Stamenkovic said: "These funds cannot last for ever."
The institute forecast trade deficit to reach $1.5-1.6 billion by the end of the year.
According to Stamenkovic current credit and monetary policy is becoming expansive. "Money supply M1 in the past four months grew quicker than prices."
In the second quarter, money supply increased by 20.4 percent to 4,049 million dinars ($826.3 million).

Stamenkovic said the upward trend continued in July when M1 rose by another 288 million dinars or 7.1 percent against June. Again, the increase was higher than inflation which rose by 6.6 percent in July, he said.

"Expansive monetary policy will inevitable lead to speeding up inflation," Stamenkovic said adding that he expected a surge in price rises at the end of the year. Annual inflation to August reached 99.2 percent. -- Gordana Kukic, Belgrade Newsroom +381 11 222 4254
